questions.stemHtml: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of pain and swelling of her hands, wrists, and knees. Physical examination shows swelling, warmth, and tenderness of several metacarpal, phalangeal, and proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally and of the wrists and knees. Serum studies show rheumatoid factor and anticyclic citrullinated polypeptide antibodies. Administration of prednisone results in clinical improvement. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the beneficial effect of this drug in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Activation of Janus kinase/STAT pathway

options.label: C
options.html: C. Activation of serine kinase/Smads pathway

options.label: E
options.html: E. Stimulation of adenylyl cyclase activity

options.label: F
options.html: F. Stimulation of guanylyl cyclase activity

options.label: G
options.html: G. Stimulation of hormone-receptor complex binding to DNA

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: G.

Educational Objective: Rheumatoid arthritis is a polyarticular inflammatory arthritis that is characterized by increased serum concentrations of rheumatoid factor. Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis may include glucocorticoids, such as prednisone, which functions to stimulate hormone-receptor complex binding to DNA.

Key Concept: Glucocorticoids such as prednisone are synthetic derivatives of endogenously produced cortisol used to treat a host of disorders including rheumatoid arthritis and various autoimmune diseases.

Explanation: Glucocorticoids exert their anti-inflammatory effect through several mechanisms, including the reduction of circulating lymphocytes and inhibiting lymphocyte migration. Prednisone binds to steroid receptors and is transported to the nucleus where it downregulates gene expression of cytokines and proinflammatory substances. When taken for prolonged periods of time, it can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis leading to a hypoadrenal crisis if exogenous corticosteroids are abruptly withdrawn. Glucocorticoid analogs also have adverse long-term effects on insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, and bone health; Cushing syndrome and osteoporosis can result following prolonged use.

Differential: The patient in this case is being administered prednisone for treatment of her rheumatoid arthritis. Prednisone functions by stimulating hormone-receptor complexes to bind to DNA.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, E, and F.

Choice A: Activation of Janus kinase/STAT pathway is incorrect. An example of a medication that functions on the Janus kinase/STAT pathway is ruxolitinib. However, ruxolitinib is an inhibitor of the Janus kinase/STAT pathway.

Choice B: Activation of phospholipase C is incorrect. Phospholipase C is a membrane-associated enzyme that functions to cleave phospholipids. Glucocorticoids do not exert their beneficial effect through this mechanism.

Choice C: Activation of serine kinase/Smads pathway is incorrect. The Smads pathway is involved with control of gene expression. Glucocorticoids function by stimulating hormone-receptor complexes to bind to DNA.

Choice D: Activation of tyrosine kinase is incorrect. Medications such as imatinib function to inhibit tyrosine kinase. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are typically used to treat various cancers.

Choice E: Stimulation of adenylyl cyclase activity is incorrect. Forskolin is an example of a plant derivative that functions to stimulate adenylyl cyclase activity. Stimulation of hormone-receptor complex binding to DNA is the more likely mechanism of the beneficial effect of prednisone in this patient.

Choice F: Stimulation of guanylyl cyclase activity is incorrect. Riociguat is an example of a medication that functions to stimulate guanylate cyclase activity. This medication may be used to treat pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stemHtml: An 18-year-old man has recurrent hematuria and a serum creatinine concentration of 1.2 mg/dL. Results of immunofluorescence studies for immunoglobulin heavy chains of a glomerulus are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: IgA nephropathy is characterized by IgA deposits in the glomerular mesangium, identified through immunofluorescence staining, and often presents with episodic hematuria following respiratory infections.

Key Concept: In IgA nephropathy, immunofluorescence staining typically shows a granular pattern of IgA deposits in the mesangium.

Explanation: IgA nephropathy, or Berger disease, is the most common form of primary glomerulonephritis globally, characterized by IgA deposition in the glomerular mesangium. It often presents with episodic hematuria following upper respiratory infections and can progress to chronic kidney disease. Diagnosis is confirmed by renal biopsy, where immunofluorescence staining shows dominant IgA deposits in the mesangium, often accompanied by C3 and IgG. The disease is thought to result from abnormal glycosylation of IgA1, leading to immune complex deposition and inflammation in the kidneys. Management typically involves controlling blood pressure and proteinuria with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, while more severe cases may require corticosteroids or immunosuppressants.

Differential: This patient presents with recurrent hematuria and an increased serum creatinine, with an immunofluorescence consistent with the deposition seen in IgA nephropathy.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Goodpasture syndrome is incorrect. Goodpasture syndrome commonly presents with hematuria and hemoptysis. Biopsy and immunofluorescence show linear IgG deposits along the glomerular basement membrane, rather than the diffuse deposit pattern seen in this patient.

Choice C: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis often presents with hematuria and proteinuria. Biopsy shows a characteristic “tram-track” appearance with granular IgG and C3 deposit.

Choice D: Membranous nephropathy is incorrect. Membranous nephropathy presents as a nephrotic syndrome. Biopsy shows a thickened glomerular basement membrane and granular IgG and C3 deposits.

Choice E: Minimal change disease is incorrect. Most commonly seen in children with nephrotic syndrome, minimal change disease will show podocyte effacement and negative immunofluorescence on biopsy analysis.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man who lives in Rhode Island comes to the physician because of intermittent fever and marked fatigue over the past 6 months. He is a frequent hunter and has had numerous tick bites on recent hunting trips. He had a splenectomy at age 15 years after an automobile collision; he received numerous blood transfusions during that hospitalization. His temperature now is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild jaundice and an evanescent, slightly erythematous, and pruritic rash. The liver is tender and palpated 6 cm below the right costal margin. Serum transaminase activities are increased. A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes and numerous ring-like structures within erythrocytes, several of which show tetrad formations. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: This New England resident with a history of splenectomy and frequent tick bites presenting with jaundice, rash, liver injury, and a peripheral blood smear with numerous intraerythrocytic tetrad forms most likely has a Babesia infection.

Evaluation: Babesiosis is a tick-borne disease transmitted by the Ixodes scapularis tick. Babesiosis classically presents with nonspecific symptoms, which can include hemolytic anemia and organ failure. Patients with a history of asplenia are predisposed to severe symptoms.

Definition: Clinical history along with identification of intraerythrocytic tetrad forms (Maltese cross) is diagnostic for babesiosis. Patients often present with fever, myalgias, arthralgias, rash, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and abnormal liver function testing (increased transaminases).

Prevention: Preventing tick bites is the cornerstone of preventing babesiosis.

Treatment: The first-line treatment is a combination of atovaquone and azithromycin for mild disease.

Differential: The differential includes tick-borne illnesses such as Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, and ehrlichiosis. Additionally, malaria should be considered in the setting of intraerythrocytic parasites on blood smear; however, the tetrad formations along with the clinical history is more consistent with babesiosis in this case.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: Borrelia burgdorferi is incorrect. B. burgdorferi causes Lyme disease and is a spirochete bacterium transmitted by the Ixodes scapularis tick. Early Lyme disease classically presents with erythema migrans at the site of the tick bite. However, Lyme disease would not cause intraerythrocytic parasites with tetrad forms.

Choice C: Hepatitis C virus is incorrect. Hepatitis C virus can present with increased hepatic transaminases and nonspecific symptoms, but would not have intraerythrocytic parasites seen on blood smear.

Choice D: Plasmodium falciparum is incorrect. P. falciparum is transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito, which would be less likely in this patient who did not recently travel to an endemic location and has noted tick exposure. While both Babesia species and P. falciparum present with intraerythrocytic parasites, the tetrad forms (Maltese cross) are more consistent with babesiosis.

Choice E: Rickettsia rickettsii is incorrect. R. rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever and is transmitted through the Dermacentor tick species. R. rickettsii primarily infects vascular endothelial cells leading to systemic vasculitis. It does not have intraerythrocytic parasites and presents classically with high fever and a characteristic rash.

questions.stemHtml: The mother of a 13-year-old boy calls the physician to seek advice. She says, "I just caught my son smoking. I am so upset. Since he's been able to talk, I've told him over and over again that smoking is bad. When he was 7 years old, he would even embarrass me in restaurants complaining about other people smoking. No one has ever smoked in our house. Now he's doing it. I've tried to talk to him and he just won't answer me. What can I do to make him stop?" When advising the mother on how to get her son to stop smoking, which of the following actions on her part will have the greatest impact?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Point out the cost of buying cigarettes

options.label: B
options.html: B. State how it will affect his appearance

options.label: C
options.html: C. Talk about the increased risk of heart problems and emphysema

options.label: D
options.html: D. Talk to the parents of her son's friends

options.label: E
options.html: E. Voice her displeasure at his smoking

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Per Erikson’s theory of psychosocial stages of development, adolescents value their appearance. As such, it can be effective to invoke appearance-related concerns when counseling for behavior change, such as with this patient.

Key Concept: When providing psychoeducation to increase a patient’s motivation to change a health behavior, physicians should bear in mind the patient’s values. Specifically, physicians should consider which stage of psychosocial development patients are in.

Explanation: Erik Erikson was a German-born American psychoanalyst who, in collaboration with his wife, Joan Erikson, proposed a theory of psychosocial stages of development. In his theory, a 13-year-old patient is navigating the “Identity versus Role Confusion” stage of psychosocial development. This stage involves the weighing of their experiences and societal expectations to determine their identity. During this stage, adolescents care about and may experiment with their appearance. As such, physicians may choose to emphasize the effects of a health behavior change on an adolescent patient’s appearance.

Differential: Physicians may also choose to invoke adolescent patients’ concerns about their peers’ opinions, another aspect of identity formation.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A and Choice C: Point out the cost of buying cigarettes and talk about the increased risk of heart problems and emphysema are incorrect. These issues typically concern adults more than adolescents.

Choice D and Choice E: Talk to the parents of her son's friends and voice her displeasure at his smoking are both incorrect. Adolescents care more about their peers’ opinions in formulating their identity than their parents’ opinions.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old primigravid woman at 17 weeks' gestation comes to the office because of a 3-week history of mild pain in her arms and hands. The pain increases in severity with physical activity and keeps her awake at night. She notes mild weakness when gripping small objects. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 17-week gestation. Which of the following additional physical findings is most likely in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Bilateral tenderness at the lateral epicondyle

options.label: B
options.html: B. Hyperreflexia of the upper extremities

options.label: C
options.html: C. Numbness restricted to the index fingers and thumbs bilaterally

options.label: D
options.html: D. Pain with percussion on the volar surface of the wrist

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common cause of hand and arm pain in pregnant patients. The Tinel test, which refers to pain with percussion on the volar surface of the wrist, is positive in carpal tunnel syndrome.

Key Concept: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel and is a common cause of wrist and hand pain in pregnant patients. A thorough physical examination is important in establishing the diagnosis.

Explanation: Carpal tunnel most commonly presents with pain, weakness, and paresthesia of the thumb and first three fingers. In addition to the Tinel test, another provocative maneuver is the Phalen test, in which symptoms are reproduced when the dorsal aspects of the palms are placed together with the wrists at 90 degrees. Patients with mild symptoms can be treated conservatively with wrist splinting and ergonomic changes, including the use of wrist support devices for patients who use the computer frequently. Patients who have persistent or severe symptoms or muscular weakness may require surgical decompression.

Differential: Pregnancy increases the risk for carpal tunnel syndrome. The median nerve affected supplies sensation to the thumb and the lateral two and a half fingers bilaterally. Her symptoms are isolated to her hands and arms, bilaterally, which decreases the likelihood of a more proximal lesion that would result in pain at the elbow or hyperreflexia.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, and C.

Choice A: Bilateral tenderness at the lateral epicondyle is incorrect. Tenderness at the lateral epicondyle occurs in tennis elbow or lateral epicondylitis. Presenting symptoms include pain in the lateral elbow with wrist extension. This patient’s pain is primarily in her hands and arms, making lateral epicondylitis unlikely.

Choice B: Hyperreflexia of the upper extremities is incorrect. Hyperreflexia of the upper extremities may be seen with abnormalities of the central nervous system such as cervical disc herniation, stroke, or multiple sclerosis. However, a lesion of the central nervous system would be unlikely to cause equal symptoms bilaterally.

Choice C: Numbness restricted to the index fingers and thumbs bilaterally is incorrect. The median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar surfaces of the thumb and lateral two and a half fingers, so pain would be expected in this distribution in carpal tunnel syndrome. Other symptoms may include paresthesias or mild weakness.

questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of weakness and fatigue. She has hypertension treated with methyldopa for the past year. Her blood pressure today is 120/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor and a uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 9 g/dL, hematocrit of 40%, reticulocyte count of 15%, and spherocytosis. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test result is positive. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the anemia in this patient?

options.label: F
options.html: F. Rh incompatibility with the fetus

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: This patient presents with hemolytic anemia 1 year after beginning therapy with methyldopa. Methyldopa is known to induce autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which presents with anemia and a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, as in this patient.

Evaluation: Patients with drug-induced hemolytic anemia present with a clinical history of use of a triggering drug and new symptoms of anemia. Results of laboratory studies will show a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test and increased reticulocyte count.

Definition: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia occurs when there are antibodies against red blood cells which result in the destruction of the red blood cells, subsequently causing anemia. There are many underlying associated triggers of autoimmune hemolytic anemia, including drugs, infections, and malignancies.

Prevention: Methyldopa is not a preferred agent for management of hypertension. Avoiding known triggers of autoimmune hemolytic anemia is the best preventive measure, though, frequently, triggers will be unknown or unexpected.

Treatment: Discontinuing methyldopa or another offending drug is the mainstay of management in hemolytic anemia triggered by drug use. In severe or persistent cases, corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive agents may be administered.

Differential: This patient with hypertension, pregnancy, and hemolytic anemia has a broad differential; however, given the patient’s 1-year history of methyldopa use, methyldopa-induced autoimmune hemolytic anemia is the most likely cause of her anemia.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, E, and F.

Choice B: Chronic glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Chronic glomerulonephritis can be associated with anemia; however, anemia would result from mechanisms such as erythropoietin deficiency, inflammation, and bone marrow suppression. Chronic glomerulonephritis would not be associated with Coombs-positive hemolysis.

Choices C and E: Folic acid deficiency and iron deficiency are incorrect. These would cause Coombs-negative macrocytic anemia and Coombs-negative microcytic anemia respectively. This patient’s positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is consistent with autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is likely to be an adverse effect of medication.

Choice D: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency would present with Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with autoimmune hemolytic anemia secondary to methyldopa use.

Choice F: Rh incompatibility with the fetus is incorrect. Rh incompatibility with the fetus occurs when maternal anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and cause hemolysis of fetal red blood cells. It causes anemia in the fetus, not in the mother.

Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: This patient presents with hemolytic anemia 1 year after beginning therapy with methyldopa. Methyldopa is known to induce autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which presents with anemia and a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, as in this patient.

Evaluation: Patients with drug-induced hemolytic anemia present with a clinical history of use of a triggering drug and new symptoms of anemia. Results of laboratory studies will show a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test and increased reticulocyte count.

Definition: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia occurs when there are antibodies against red blood cells which result in the destruction of the red blood cells, subsequently causing anemia. There are many underlying associated triggers of autoimmune hemolytic anemia, including drugs, infections, and malignancies.

Prevention: Methyldopa is not a preferred agent for management of hypertension. Avoiding known triggers of autoimmune hemolytic anemia is the best preventive measure, though, frequently, triggers will be unknown or unexpected.

Treatment: Discontinuing methyldopa or another offending drug is the mainstay of management in hemolytic anemia triggered by drug use. In severe or persistent cases, corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive agents may be administered.

Differential: This patient with hypertension, pregnancy, and hemolytic anemia has a broad differential; however, given the patient’s 1-year history of methyldopa use, methyldopa-induced autoimmune hemolytic anemia is the most likely cause of her anemia.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, E, and F.

Choice B: Chronic glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Chronic glomerulonephritis can be associated with anemia; however, anemia would result from mechanisms such as erythropoietin deficiency, inflammation, and bone marrow suppression. Chronic glomerulonephritis would not be associated with Coombs-positive hemolysis.

Choices C and E: Folic acid deficiency and iron deficiency are incorrect. These would cause Coombs-negative macrocytic anemia and Coombs-negative microcytic anemia respectively. This patient’s positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is consistent with autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is likely to be an adverse effect of medication.

Choice D: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency would present with Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with autoimmune hemolytic anemia secondary to methyldopa use.

Choice F: Rh incompatibility with the fetus is incorrect. Rh incompatibility with the fetus occurs when maternal anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and cause hemolysis of fetal red blood cells. It causes anemia in the fetus, not in the mother.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of the anemia in this patient?

questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician because of thickening of his skin, diarrhea, and weight loss during the past 6 months. Physical examination shows generalized hyperkeratotic skin lesions. Serum concentrations of antiendomysial and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are increased. Stool analysis shows an increased fat concentration. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the deficiency causing this patient's skin lesions?

options.label: D
options.html: D. Decreased production of bile acids

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: This patient is presenting with celiac disease, steatorrhea, and hyperkeratotic skin lesions most consistent with vitamin A deficiency. Patients with celiac disease have malabsorption of fat, and therefore, are at risk for deficiencies of the fat soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K).

Evaluation: Vitamin A deficiency can stem from untreated celiac disease that leads to fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.

Definition: Deficiency in vitamin A can present with a variety of symptoms, including nonspecific dermatologic problems such as hyperkeratosis, as seen in this patient.

Prevention: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disease and prevention is unknown. However, preventing symptoms and complications of the disease involves adherence to a gluten-free diet.

Treatment: Celiac disease can be modified and treated with dietary changes, such as omission of gluten and gluten-containing foods.

Differential: This patient with celiac disease and steatorrhea along with new, hyperkeratotic skin lesions likely has vitamin A deficiency.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Abnormal lymphatics is incorrect. These are seen in lesions such as lymphangiomas, which are benign malformations of the lymphatic system that can cause soft, well circumscribed lesions. They are not hyperkeratotic and are not associated with celiac disease.

Choice B: Bacterial overgrowth is incorrect. In the intestine, this can cause bloating, discomfort, and gastrointestinal symptoms similar to celiac disease. However, bacterial overgrowth would not present with increased concentrations of anti-endomysial and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies.

Choice C: Decreased lipase secretion is incorrect. This can be seen in pathology such as chronic pancreatitis, which would present with chronic abdominal pain and steatorrhea. It would not present with increased levels of anti-endomysial and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies.

Choice D: Decreased production of bile acids is incorrect. This can be seen in primary biliary cholangitis, which contributes to fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. However, the increased anti-endomysial and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies make mucosal dysfunction the most likely cause.

questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of fatigue and muscle weakness. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show a calcium concentration of 11.8 mg/dL and intact parathyroid hormone concentration of 340 pg/mL. A nuclear parathyroid scan is shown; the arrow indicates a parathyroid adenoma in the region of the right lower pole of the thyroid gland. This adenoma is most likely located in which of the following labeled areas of the axial CT scan of the thyroid gland?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: The parathyroid glands are four small endocrine glands located on the posterior surface of the thyroid, near the superior and inferior poles.

Key Concept: The parathyroid glands are four small, encapsulated endocrine glands located on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, embedded within its connective tissue. They are positioned near the superior and inferior poles of the thyroid lobes, with two glands on each side, though anatomical variations are common.

Explanation: The parathyroid glands are closely associated with the recurrent laryngeal nerves, which traverse near the tracheoesophageal groove. Additionally, the inferior thyroid arteries, branches of the thyrocervical trunk, provide vascular supply to the parathyroid glands. The glands are responsible for regulating calcium homeostasis in the body through the secretion of parathyroid hormone.

Differential: This patient has a right-sided parathyroid adenoma, which on transverse CT scan would be present just posterior to the right lobe of the thyroid.  

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: A is incorrect. A points to the musculature anterior to the thyroid gland.

Choice C: C is incorrect. C points to the far lateral edge of the thyroid gland.

Choice D: D is incorrect. D points to the right lobe of the thyroid gland.

Choice E: E is incorrect. E points to the tissue between the sternocleidomastoid muscle and the internal jugular vein.

questions.stemHtml: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of fever, sore throat, palpitations, and intermittent pain and swelling of multiple joints. She does not appear to be in acute distress. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a pericardial friction rub, a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur, and redness and swelling of the left knee. Laboratory studies show an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and antistreptolysin O antibodies. A throat culture grows no organisms. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly. Echocardiography shows multiple 0.3-cm vegetations on the mitral valve. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of the valvular heart disease in this patient?

options.label: B
options.html: B. Coagulation necrosis as a result of bacterial invasion

options.label: D
options.html: D. Leaflet destruction by bacterial exotoxin

options.label: E
options.html: E. Myomatous degeneration caused by proteoglycan deposition

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Educational Objective: This patient’s fever, sore throat, palpitations, joint swelling, murmur, and valvular vegetations are consistent with acute rheumatic fever. Acute rheumatic fever is a result of injury from cross-reactive antibodies.

Evaluation: Rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthralgia, pancarditis (pericarditis, myocarditis, and endocarditis), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea, fever, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and short PR interval on ECG following an infection from group A β-hemolytic streptococci (frequently pharyngitis).

Definition: In rheumatic fever, antibodies against M protein can cross-react with self-antigens, such as myosin and other antigens found on the pericardium, myocardium, and endocardium. The deposition of antibodies on the mitral or tricuspid valve causes inflammation and fibrosis, which may lead to regurgitation initially and then stenosis if untreated.

Prevention: Rheumatic fever may be prevented by identifying and treating streptococcal infections.

Treatment: Treatment of rheumatic fever includes treating the associated infection with penicillin as first-line therapy.

Differential: In this patient, fever, sore throat, palpitations, joint swelling, murmur, and valvular vegetations narrows the differential to rheumatic fever, which is believed to arise from antibody cross-reactivity caused by molecular mimicry.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Choice A: Antigen-antibody complex deposition is incorrect. Antigen-antibody complex deposition is associated with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis but is not the mechanism of rheumatic fever. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is commonly associated with streptococcal pharyngeal or skin infection.

Choice B: Coagulation necrosis as a result of bacterial invasion is incorrect. Coagulation necrosis is caused by ischemia or infarction of local tissue. While coagulation necrosis can be the result of sepsis or other bacterial infection, rheumatic fever is caused by cross-reactive antibodies.

Choice D: Leaflet destruction by bacterial exotoxin is incorrect. Bacterial exotoxin release is the cause of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Exotoxin triggers the sloughing of skin at the granular layer of the epidermis. Clinically, scalded skin syndrome manifests following impetigo, which is a common superficial infection in young children.

Choice E: Myxomatous degeneration caused by proteoglycan deposition is incorrect. Myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve is associated with the development of mitral valve prolapse. Mitral valve prolapse is associated with mitral regurgitation but is not associated with acute rheumatic fever.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the police found him collapsed and unresponsive in an alleyway. He is known to have alcohol use disorder and use intravenous illicit drugs. Physical examination shows jaundice and multiple widespread cutaneous ecchymoses. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 160,000/mm3, prothrombin time of 20 seconds (INR=3), and partial thromboplastin time of 55 seconds. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following steps in procoagulant protein synthesis is most likely defective in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: This patient’s presenting symptoms of thrombocytopenia, increased INR, and jaundice in the setting of heavy alcohol and intravenous substance use, are most consistent with underlying cirrhosis of the liver. The patient has an increased INR and partial thromboplastin time, which is likely due to defective gamma carboxylation causing decreased synthesis of procoagulant factors.

Evaluation: Coagulopathy in cirrhosis clinically presents with easy bruising and predisposition for bleeding complications.

Definition: Laboratory findings of coagulopathy in cirrhosis include increased partial thromboplastin time and INR, which occur secondary to synthetic dysfunction of the liver’s production of vitamin K dependent coagulation factors. Gamma carboxylation is an enzymatic process conducted in the liver that renders the vitamin K dependent coagulation factors active.

Prevention: Prevention of this complication includes preventing cirrhosis from occurring, counseling regarding alcohol use, and providing social support to mitigate the consequences of excessive alcohol use.

Treatment: In the setting of acute bleeding and need for transient normalization of the coagulation cascade, prothrombin complex concentrate can be administered.

Differential: This patient with cirrhosis from alcohol use likely has coagulopathy secondary to cirrhosis. Cirrhosis causes decreased gamma carboxylation and subsequent activation of the vitamin K dependent coagulation factors. Further complicating this patient’s differential is the reality that they may already have a vitamin K deficiency as well. Therefore, when treating this patient, one would give empiric vitamin K repletion and measure the coagulation concentrations to determine if they normalize with repletion of the vitamin K. If they remain abnormal, this makes coagulopathy secondary to cirrhosis even more likely. 

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Disulfide bond formation is incorrect. This is a mechanism of covalent bonds between cysteine residues that occurs in the post-translational modification of proteins. It is not directly affected by cirrhosis.

Choice C: N-glycosylation is incorrect. It is a mechanism in the post-translational modification of proteins which involves the enzymatic addition of oligosaccharides to proteins and is not directly affected by cirrhosis.

Choice D: Transpeptidation is incorrect. It occurs when there is formation of peptide bonds between amino acids, which is a mechanism that is used in bacterial cell wall synthesis and is a target of some antibiotics.Choice E: Ubiquitination is incorrect. This is a post-translational medication process where ubiquitin is covalently bonded to a protein. It is not defective in cirrhosis.

questions.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man is diagnosed with acute myelogenous leukemia. He has no personal or family history of major medical illness. He has never smoked. He has worked at a local oil refinery for the past 20 years. The patient believes that his leukemia was caused by exposure to chemicals at his job. He tells the physician, "If you write a letter to my employer stating that my illness was caused by something I was exposed to at my job, then workers' compensation will pay for my treatment and provide me with some income to help care for my family. Can you help me?" Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: A. "I suspect that you can make a strong case for workers' compensation eligibility on your own."

options.label: B
options.html: B. "I will refer you to an oncologist and you can discuss with him the likelihood that this was caused by a chemical exposure."

options.label: C
options.html: C. "I'm sorry, but it's unlikely that your occupation contributed to the development of this type of leukemia."

options.label: D
options.html: D. "We'll need to analyze your blood for certain chemicals first to see if your body absorbed them."

options.label: E
options.html: E. "What type of work do you do at the refinery?"

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: To write effective letters on patients’ behalf, physicians should first gather a thorough history to provide evidence for their positions. The most appropriate initial response to this patient would be to ask more about his work to learn more about any potential occupational exposures.

Key Concept: Patients may request that physicians write various letters to excuse them from certain activities or provide certain benefits (eg, workers’ compensation letters, service animal letters, etc.). Physicians should gather a thorough history prior to agreeing to write a letter.

Explanation: To write an accurate and helpful workers’ compensation letter, the physician needs to provide objective evidence that the patient’s medical condition was or was not caused by working conditions. The physician should also only comment within their area of expertise and use evidence-based medicine. Physicians may decline to write a letter if it requires them to comment on medical issues outside of their expertise.

Differential: Though laboratory studies or imaging studies may assist in establishing or refuting a workers’ compensation claim, the physician in this case should first gather a thorough history.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: "I suspect that you can make a strong case for workers' compensation eligibility on your own" is inappropriate. Workers’ compensation cases require a physician’s letter. The physician should explore the patient’s request and gather a history.

Choice B: "I will refer you to an oncologist and you can discuss with him the likelihood that this was caused by a chemical exposure" is premature. Prior to placing a referral, the physician should gather a history, which will inform whether a referral is appropriate.

Choice C: "I'm sorry, but it's unlikely that your occupation contributed to the development of this type of leukemia" is a premature statement. The physician should first gather a history to determine whether the patient’s occupation may have contributed to his illness.

Choice D: "We'll need to analyze your blood for certain chemicals first to see if your body absorbed them" is premature. The physician should first gather a history to determine whether further testing is warranted.

questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after fainting while playing basketball. There was no trauma or evidence of seizure activity when he fainted. He has a history of a benign, low-grade cardiac murmur that had been attributed to his fitness as an athlete. He is now conscious. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F), pulse is 62/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg. There is no cyanosis. The lungs are clear. Cardiac examination shows a double impulse over the carotid arteries. There are normal pulses in the extremities. S1 and S2 are normal, but there is a grade 3/6, systolic ejection murmur heard best in the second intercostal space at the left parasternal border and into the apex. The murmur increases in intensity on Valsalva maneuver. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s murmur?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: This otherwise healthy, athletic patient with a murmur exacerbated in states of low preload (eg, Valsalva maneuver) most likely has hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). In HOCM, subaortic septal prominence causes dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction, producing a characteristic systolic murmur.

Evaluation: HOCM typically presents with syncope or sudden cardiac death in otherwise healthy, young athletic patients. HOCM should be suspected in any athlete with a suspicious murmur (ie, exacerbated in low preload states) or unexplained syncope, in patients with family history, or in patients with ECG or echocardiographic findings suggestive of left ventricular septal hypertrophy.

Definition: HOCM, which is suspected to follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, leads to hypertrophy of myocytes and results in subaortic septal prominence within the LVOT. Due to the narrowed LVOT, any hemodynamic influence that prevents the stenting open of the tract (eg, low preload leading to low stroke volume due to Valsalva maneuver, standing, or hypovolemia) will result in an exacerbation of the murmur because of increased turbulent blood flow. Significant derangements in hemodynamics can cause complete obstruction of the LVOT, causing obstruction by abnormal motion of the mitral valve. Resultant decrease in cardiac output leads to syncope. Arrhythmogenic foci are also a common cause of mortality in HOCM. The condition is diagnosed with echocardiography.

Prevention: The condition is idiopathic in many patients, thus there is no consistent preventive measure. Secondary prevention occurs through screening ECG with confirmatory echocardiography.

Treatment: Treatment focuses on prevention of symptoms and complications. Treatment commonly includes the use of β-adrenergic blockers and antiarrhythmics, placement of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, and surgical procedures, such as mitral clipping and myomectomy.

Differential: Differential diagnoses include valvular heart disease and other forms of cardiomyopathy. In this example, the differential can be narrowed to HOCM based on the patient’s young age and risk factors, plus consistent murmur.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Bicuspid aortic valve is incorrect. Bicuspid aortic valve presents with a systolic crescendo decrescendo murmur best heard in the aortic listening area, which is usually decreased in intensity with preload-limiting maneuvers. There is often a family history of the condition. This patient’s murmur is not consistent with bicuspid aortic valve.

Choice B: Mitral valve prolapse is incorrect. Mitral valve prolapse presents with a midsystolic click heard best over the mitral listening area.

Choice C: Pulmonary stenosis is not the best choice. Pulmonary stenosis presents with a systolic murmur best heard in the second left intercostal region, which is often crescendo decrescendo, though quieter and with less radiation to the lower neck by comparison to aortic stenosis. Pulmonic stenosis is typically seen in the setting of tetralogy of Fallot. Pulmonic stenosis murmur would be decreased in intensity with Valsalva maneuver.

Choice E: Ventricular septal defect is not the best choice. Ventricular septal defect presents with a holosystolic murmur heard at the midsternal border and would be present from birth.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man has a 7-month history of fatigue and abdominal discomfort. Examination shows splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. A complete blood count shows anemia, teardrop erythrocytes, and a leukoerythroblastic reaction. A bone marrow biopsy shows myelofibrosis. Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen on microscopic examination of tissue from the spleen?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Decrease of both red and white pulp

options.label: B
options.html: B. Enlargement of the white pulp

options.label: C
options.html: C. Erythrophagocytosis in the splenic cords

options.label: D
options.html: D. Prominent collections of lipid-filled macrophages

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: This patient with hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and a bone marrow biopsy with myelofibrosis most likely has primary myelofibrosis. Due to the bone marrow’s inability to conduct normal hematopoiesis, patients often develop extramedullary hematopoiesis, typically in the spleen.

Evaluation: Primary myelofibrosis, also known as myeloid metaplasia with myelofibrosis, classically presents with anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and leukoerythroblastic blood smear.

Definition: Diagnosis of myelofibrosis occurs via a bone marrow biopsy showing fibrosis. Supportive studies include cytogenetics that would identify mutations such as JAK2 that can lead to the disease.

Prevention: There is no known prevention for primary myelofibrosis.

Treatment: Treatment depends on severity and cause. A potential treatment is ruxolitinib, a Janus kinase inhibitor.

Differential: This patient with anemia, a bone marrow biopsy with myelofibrosis, and hepatosplenomegaly likely has primary myelofibrosis and is undergoing extramedullary trilineage hematopoiesis in his spleen. 

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Decrease of both red and white pulp is incorrect. Decrease of both red and white pulp is seen in splenic atrophy, which is a severe manifestation of splenic hypofunction and can be seen in diseases such as celiac disease.

Choice B: Enlargement of the white pulp is incorrect. Enlargement of the white pulp can be seen in common variable immunodeficiency, which presents with low concentrations of immunoglobulins and recurrent infection.

Choice C: Erythrophagocytosis in the splenic cords is incorrect. Erythrophagocytosis in the splenic cords is a hallmark feature of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, which is a severe inflammatory disorder that causes acute and critical illness. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with primary myelofibrosis.

Choice D: Prominent collections of lipid-filled macrophages is incorrect. Lipid-filled macrophages can occur in Gaucher disease, which is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme β-glucosidase. This patient’s age and presentation is inconsistent with Gaucher disease.

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because of insomnia since her fiancé suddenly broke off their engagement 10 days ago. She has difficulty falling asleep, but once she is asleep she usually sleeps well. Taking hot baths, drinking chamomile tea, and listening to soothing music before bed have not resulted in relief. She states that her lack of sleep is beginning to affect her performance at work, and she asks for medication to help her temporarily. If the physician determines that pharmacotherapy to help this patient sleep is indicated, the most appropriate medication has which of the following mechanisms of action?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Enhances the action of AMPA-type glutamate receptors

options.label: B
options.html: B. Enhances γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) action by increasing the frequency of channel openings

options.label: C
options.html: C. Facilitates central nervous system excitation

options.label: D
options.html: D. Increases the action of GABA by increasing the duration of channel openings

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic medications such as zolpidem, are used to treat insomnia by enhancing the action of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), which increases the frequency of chloride channel openings at the GABAA receptor. This is the most appropriate medication for this patient because it decreases sleep latency and wake time after sleep onset without affecting sleep architecture other than increasing time spent in stage N2 sleep.

Key Concept: Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic medications (eg, zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) are known to increase sleep time and can be used temporarily to address insomnia in patients with adjustment disorder.

Explanation: Similar to benzodiazepines, nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic medications bind GABA subunits to increase the frequency of channel openings, thus potentiating GABA activity. GABA receptors allow influx of chloride ions, which hyperpolarizes neurons and thus slows neuronal firing, producing a calming and soporific effect.

Differential: Barbiturates increase the action of GABA by increasing the duration of channel openings. However, barbiturates are not commonly used for insomnia as they have long half-lives and may produce daytime sleepiness.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choices A, C, and E: Enhances the action of AMPA-type glutamate receptors, facilitates central nervous system excitation, and increases glutamate-induced depolarization are incorrect. These choices all increase neuronal firing and put patients at risk for glutamate excitotoxicity, which would not lead to a calming effect.

Choice D: Increases the action of GABA by increasing the duration of channel openings is incorrect. Barbiturates increase the action of GABA by increasing the duration of channel openings. However, barbiturates are not commonly used for insomnia as they have long half-lives and may produce daytime sleepiness.

questions.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after his left forearm was slashed with a pocketknife during a bar fight. Continuous application of pressure to the affected area has not resolved the profuse bleeding. His pulse is 140/min, and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pale conjunctivae. Examination of the left upper extremity shows a 3-cm laceration that is oriented transversely over the palmar aspect of the distal forearm and located 2 cm proximal to the distal palmar wrist crease. He is unable to abduct the left thumb or flex the metacarpophalangeal or proximal interphalangeal joints of the index and middle fingers. He is able to flex the distal interphalangeal joints of all digits, including the thumb. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the palmar aspect of the thumb and index and middle fingers. Capillary refill time is normal for all digits. Doppler pulse evaluation of the superficial palmar arch shows an intact signal. A median nerve injury is suspected. Which of the following tendons also is most likely injured in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Injury to the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendons may result in the inability to flex the proximal interphalangeal joints. The abnormalities on examination identified in this patient may be due to a combination of a distal median nerve injury as well as injury to the index and middle finger FDS tendons.

Evaluation: Injury to the FDS tendons may result in deficits or difficulties with flexion of the proximal interphalangeal joints of the index to little fingers.

Definition: The FDS muscle originates from the medial epicondyle and the shaft of the radius with innervation provided by the median nerve. The FDS muscle has individual tendons that attach to the index to little fingers to allow for flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joints. The FDS tendons travel through the carpal tunnel with the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and flexor pollicis longus (FPL) as well as the median nerve.

Prevention: FDS tendon injuries may be prevented through avoidance of trauma.

Treatment: Treatment of a ruptured or cut tendon often involves surgical intervention.

Differential: The patient in this case has signs of distal median nerve injury including the inability to abduct the thumb or flex the metacarpophalangeal joints of the index and middle fingers with sensory deficits in the median nerve distribution. The inability of the patient to flex the proximal interphalangeal joints of the index and middle fingers is likely secondary to injury of the FDS tendons to those respective fingers.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Abductor pollicis longus (APL) tendon is incorrect. The APL muscle originates from the radius, ulna, and interosseous membrane. The APL functions to abduct the thumb and extend the first carpometacarpal joint.

Choice B: The flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) tendon is not the most likely injured. The FCU originates from the posterior border of the ulna and inserts at the base of the pisiform bone, hook of hamate, and the base of the fifth metacarpal. The FCU functions to flex and adduct the hand.

Choice C: Flexor digitorum profundus tendons is incorrect. The FDP is a deep muscle of the anterior forearm. The FDP provides the ability to flex the distal interphalangeal joints of the index to little fingers.

Choice E: Flexor pollicis longus tendon is not the most likely injured. The FPL originates from the radius and interosseous membrane. The main function of the FPL muscle is to flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb.

Three months ago she underwent operative removal of a catecholamine-secreting tumor from the right adrenal gland. Her mother has retinal angiomas and her maternal grandfather had a hemangioblastoma of the cerebellum. Physical examination shows a well-healed laparoscopic scar on the abdomen. This patient most likely has a mutation of which of the following genes?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: Key features of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease include multiple hemangioblastomas in the central nervous system and/or retinas, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytomas, and a family history of VHL-related tumors, as seen in this patient.

Key Concept: VHL disease is a hereditary condition characterized by the development of multiple benign and malignant tumors, particularly hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytomas.

Explanation: VHL disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 3p25-26, which leads to dysregulation of hypoxia-inducible factor and subsequent tumorigenesis. The disease is characterized by the development of highly vascular tumors such as hemangioblastomas in the central nervous system and retinas, which can present with symptoms like headaches, ataxia, and visual disturbances due to tumor location and growth. Patients are also at increased risk for renal cell carcinoma, particularly of the clear cell subtype, often necessitating nephron-sparing surgeries to manage the risk for metastasis while preserving renal function. questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of intermittent diarrhea and nausea without vomiting. The symptoms occur in the mornings before work and sometimes cause him to be late or stay home. The diarrhea is brown and loose with no traces of blood. The symptoms subside on the weekends. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following questions by the physician is most likely to be helpful in establishing the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: A. "Are you exposed to any toxins at work?"

options.label: B
options.html: B. "Do you use alcohol on a regular basis?"

options.label: C
options.html: C. "Does anyone in your family have the same symptoms?"

options.label: D
options.html: D. "How do you feel about your job these days?"

options.label: E
options.html: E. "Is anyone at work feeling ill?"

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Assessing stress-induced diarrhea involves correlating gastrointestinal symptoms with stress levels primarily through thorough patient history. For this patient, who experiences symptoms just before work, learning more about his current work-related stressors is most likely to be helpful in establishing a diagnosis.

Key Concept: Stress-induced diarrhea, particularly in the context of work-related stress, is a complex physiological reaction involving the interplay between the nervous and endocrine systems, resulting in increased bowel motility and fluid secretion.

Explanation: Stress-induced diarrhea is a physiological response where stress activates the autonomic nervous system, particularly the sympathetic branch, resulting in increased intestinal motility and secretion. During stress, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is activated, releasing corticotropin-releasing hormone and cortisol, which can alter gut permeability and influence the enteric nervous system. This hormonal cascade can lead to accelerated transit time in the intestines and increased secretion of fluids, contributing to diarrhea. For diagnosis, physicians should conduct a thorough history and physical examination, focusing on the correlation of symptoms with work-related stressors, and consider psychological assessments to evaluate stress levels. Additionally, ruling out other causes of diarrhea is essential.

Differential: This patient presents with weekday diarrhea immediately before work, with absence of symptoms on weekends. This is consistent with stress-induced diarrhea, as once the stimulus (ie, work) is removed, the patient’s symptoms resolve.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: "Are you exposed to any toxins at work?" is incorrect. While toxins can lead to diarrhea and other health concerns, it would be expected that the patient would have diarrhea after his exposures, and symptom resolution on weekends would not be expected.

Choice B: "Do you use alcohol on a regular basis?" is incorrect. Alcohol consumption can affect gastrointestinal health; however, this patient’s symptoms are only present on workdays, which makes this less likely the cause.

Choice C: "Does anyone in your family have the same symptoms?" is incorrect. This question assesses illnesses or exposures at home, which very commonly can result in diarrhea. Diarrhea from these causes would not be expected to resolve on weekends.

Choice E: "Is anyone at work feeling ill?" is incorrect. This question seeks to identify a contagious or workplace-related illness, which could cause similar issues. However, this would be highly unusual to cause persistent symptoms for 2 months.

questions.stemHtml: A 10-year-old African American boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-hour history of severe abdominal pain. He appears in acute distress. Physical examination shows pale mucous membranes. Bowel sounds are normal, and there is no rebound tenderness. His hemoglobin concentration is 8 g/dL and hematocrit is 25%. A photomicrograph of a peripheral blood smear is shown. Which of the following hemoglobin abnormalities is the most likely cause of the findings in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Impairment of the translation of the globin α-chain in erythrocyte precursor cells

options.label: B
options.html: B. Impairment of the translation of the globin β-chain in erythroid precursor cells

options.label: C
options.html: C. Misassembly of the mutant globin β-chain into α2β2 heterotetramers in erythrocytes

options.label: D
options.html: D. Misfolding of the mutant globin α-chain in the endoplasmic reticulum of reticulocytes

options.label: E
options.html: E. Misfolding of the mutant globin β-chain in the endoplasmic reticulum of reticulocytes

options.label: F
options.html: F. Polymerization of mutant α2β2 heterotetramers in erythrocytes

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: F.

Educational Objective: This 10-year-old boy presenting with acute abdominal pain, anemia, and a peripheral smear notable for red blood cell sickling likely has sickle cell disease (SCD), which occurs because of polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin S.

Evaluation: SCD classically presents with recurrent episodes of severe pain, anemia, and complications such as acute chest syndrome and avascular necrosis.

Definition: SCD is caused by mutations in globin genes that result in abnormal hemoglobin S, which polymerizes in the setting of hypoxia and causes sickling of erythrocytes. This leads to hemolysis and vaso-occlusion, which causes symptoms such as severe abdominal pain.

Prevention: There is no prevention for SCD, but prevention of sickle cell crises can be done by avoiding conditions that would cause hypoxia, along with focusing on hydration, infection prevention, blood transfusions if necessary, and avoiding triggers.

Treatment: One of the most common medications used to treat SCD is hydroxyurea, which increases fetal hemoglobin and decreases sickling and pain crises.

Differential: This patient with anemia, abdominal pain, and sickling red blood cells on peripheral smear most likely has SCD. While a child with anemia and abdominal pain portends a large differential diagnosis, the presence of sickled red blood cells on peripheral smears narrows the differential and makes SCD likely.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E.

Choices A and D: Impairment of the translation of the globin α-chain in erythrocyte precursor cells and misfolding of the mutant globin α-chain in the endoplasmic reticulum of reticulocytes are incorrect. These describe potential mechanisms of α-thalassemia. α-Thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder that has variable presentations depending on genetic profile and carrier status. α-Thalassemia typically presents with anemia but does not have pain crises such as sickle cell and would not have sickling seen on peripheral smear.

Choice B, Choice C, and Choice E: Impairment of the translation of the globin β-chain in erythroid precursor cells, misassembly of the mutant globin β-chain into α2β2 heterotetramers in erythrocytes, and misfolding of the mutant globin β-chain in the endoplasmic reticulum of reticulocytes are incorrect. These are potential mechanisms that result in β-thalassemia, which has variable presentation based on genetic profile. β-Thalassemia classically presents with microcytic anemia of variable severity. It does not have pain crises such as sickle cell and would not show sickling of red blood cells on peripheral smear.

A 36-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-year history of progressive fatigue and weakness as well as decreased appetite and intermittent nausea. She also has had a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss during this time. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are shown:
Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL
Hematocrit 34%
Serum
 Na+ 132 mEq/L
 K+ 5.7 mEq/L
 Glucose [fasting] 55 mg/dL
 Adrenocorticotropic hormone 300 pg/mL (N<120)
Which of the following histopathologic changes is most likely in this patient's adrenal cortex?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Deposition of amyloid with epithelial atrophy

options.label: B
options.html: B. Granulomatous inflammation with epithelial atrophy

options.label: C
options.html: C. Hemorrhage with islands of degenerating atrophic epithelial cells

options.label: D
options.html: D. Mononuclear cell infiltrate with epithelial atrophy

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: The most common cause of adrenocortical insufficiency is an autoimmune disease. Histopathologic examination would most likely show mononuclear cell infiltrate with epithelial atrophy, reflecting lymphocytic destruction of the adrenal cortex and resulting in cortical atrophy and loss of steroid-producing cells.

Key Concept: Adrenocortical insufficiency, commonly referred to as Addison disease, is a condition where the adrenal glands fail to produce adequate amounts of vital hormones, particularly cortisol and aldosterone.

Explanation: Clinically, patients may present with symptoms like fatigue, muscle weakness, weight loss, low blood pressure, and hyperpigmentation of the skin. The condition can be caused by autoimmune destruction, infections like tuberculosis, or metastatic cancer affecting the adrenal cortex. On histopathologic examination, the adrenal cortex in autoimmune disease typically shows lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of adrenal cortical cells. The cortex may appear atrophied with a loss of the normal zonal architecture.

Differential: This patient presents with fatigue, weakness, weight loss, and laboratory values that are remarkable for hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and increased adrenocorticotropic hormone. These findings are consistent with adrenocortical insufficiency. The most common cause is due to autoimmune destruction, which would show lymphocytic infiltrate on histopathologic examination.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Deposition of amyloid with epithelial atrophy is incorrect. Amyloid deposition is associated with amyloidosis, where protein deposits accumulate in organs and tissues, rather than being a feature of adrenal gland disorders like Addison disease.

Choice B: Granulomatous inflammation with epithelial atrophy is incorrect. Granulomatous inflammation is typically linked to infections, such as tuberculosis or sarcoidosis, rather than the autoimmune processes most involved in Addison disease.

Choice C: Hemorrhage with islands of degenerating atrophic epithelial cells is incorrect. Hemorrhage is not typically seen in adrenal cortical conditions like Addison disease. Such findings might be indicative of conditions like adrenal hemorrhage, which can occur due to severe stress, sepsis, or anticoagulation therapy.

Choice E: Necrosis of epithelial cells is incorrect. Necrosis suggests tissue death due to factors like ischemia or toxins, which is not a characteristic process in conditions such as Addison disease.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician after skin blisters appeared following exposure to the sun 2 days ago. Physical examination shows vesicles and bullae on the face, hands, upper and lower extremities, and feet. Urine studies show increased concentrations of porphyrins. This patient most likely has a defect in which of the following biochemical pathways?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is caused by a deficiency in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), disrupting the heme biosynthesis pathway and resulting in porphyrin accumulation that leads to photosensitivity and skin blistering.

Key Concept: Patients with PCT typically present with blistering, fragility, and hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed skin areas as a result of photosensitivity. 

Explanation: PCT is characterized by a disruption in the heme biosynthesis pathway due to a deficiency in the enzyme UROD. This enzymatic defect leads to the accumulation of uroporphyrin and other carboxylated porphyrins, primarily in the liver, which are then transported to the skin and excreted in urine. The buildup of these porphyrins causes photosensitivity, resulting in blistering, fragility, and hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed skin areas. Factors such as alcohol consumption, estrogen use, hepatitis C infection, and iron overload can exacerbate the condition by further inhibiting UROD activity or increasing oxidative stress. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting increased concentrations of uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin in the urine, indicative of the disrupted heme synthesis process. 

Differential: This patient is presenting with vesicles and bullae on sun exposed areas, after sun exposure 2 days prior. The increase in urine porphyrins confirms the diagnosis of PCT, which is a defect in heme biosynthesis.  

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, F, G, and H.

Choice A: Bilirubin biosynthesis is incorrect. Errors in bilirubin biosynthesis can lead to conditions like Crigler-Najjar syndrome, where patients present with severe jaundice due to excessive unconjugated bilirubin in the blood.

Choice B: Bilirubin degradation is incorrect. Disorders in bilirubin degradation, such as Dubin-Johnson syndrome, result in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, presenting with jaundice and darkly pigmented liver.

Choice C: DNA repair is incorrect. Defects in DNA repair mechanisms, as seen in xeroderma pigmentosum, lead to extreme sensitivity to UV light and a high predisposition to skin cancers. This would be expected to be diagnosed earlier in life than the presenting patient.

Choice D: DNA synthesis is incorrect. Errors in DNA synthesis can manifest as megaloblastic anemia, commonly due to vitamin B12 (cobalamin) or folate deficiency, presenting with fatigue, pallor, and macrocytic red blood cells.

Choice F: Heme degradation is incorrect. Impairments in heme degradation, such as in Gilbert's syndrome, result in mild jaundice due to the accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin.

Choice G: Nucleotide biosynthesis is incorrect. Deficiencies in nucleotide biosynthesis, like in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, cause neurologic and behavioral abnormalities, along with self-mutilating behaviors due to defective purine salvage.

Choice H: Nucleotide degradation is incorrect. Abnormalities in nucleotide degradation, such as in adenosine deaminase deficiency, lead to severe combined immunodeficiency, presenting with recurrent infections and failure to thrive.

questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 5-day history of nasal congestion, sore throat, nonproductive cough, and malaise. Evaluation shows an upper respiratory tract infection. The physician advises the mother that the patient should begin feeling better during the next few days with continued rest; he also tells the mother to ensure that the patient drinks plenty of fluids so that she stays well hydrated. The mother asks the physician, "Aren't you going to give her an antibiotic?" The physician declines, telling the mother that an antibiotic is not necessary in this case. The mother angrily responds, "Look, I know my daughter, and I know that she needs an antibiotic." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: A. "Help me to understand why it's so important to you that I give your daughter an antibiotic for this illness."

options.label: B

questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man occasionally takes a vasodilator drug sublingually to relieve chest pain due to angina pectoris. After taking this drug, the activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely increased in the coronary vascular smooth muscle cells of this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Guanylyl cyclase activity is increased in the coronary vascular smooth muscle cells of this patient after taking a vasodilator drug (likely a nitrate, such as nitroglycerin) as a relief for angina. This enzyme is activated by nitric oxide (NO), leading to increased production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP), which promotes smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

Key Concept: Guanylyl cyclase is an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of guanosine triphosphate to cyclic GMP, which mediates smooth muscle relaxation and thereby promotes vasodilation.

Explanation: This patient is taking a sublingual nitrate, likely nitroglycerin, for relief of angina pectoris. Nitroglycerin is metabolized to NO, which activates guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle resulting in muscle relaxation and vasodilation via increased intracellular cyclic GMP. This mechanism is key to relieving angina symptoms by improving oxygen delivery to ischemic myocardial tissue.

Differential: Nitrates specifically target vascular smooth muscle via the NO-guanylyl cyclase-cyclic GMP pathway. Increased guanylyl cyclase activity is central to this process, leading to vasodilation.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Adenylyl cyclase is incorrect. Adenylyl cyclase is activated in other signaling pathways, such as those involving β-adrenergic receptors, but it is not directly involved in the action of nitrates.

Choice C: Nitric oxide synthase is incorrect. NO synthase produces NO endogenously.

Choice D: Phospholipase C is incorrect. Phospholipase C is involved in G-protein coupled receptor signaling that leads to increased intracellular calcium and protein kinase C activity. In vascular smooth muscle cells, increased phospholipase C leading to protein kinase C activity results in increased smooth muscle contraction, which leads to vasoconstriction.

Choice E: Phospholipase D is incorrect. Phospholipase D plays a role in other signaling pathways but has no role in NO-induced smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with a history of angina pectoris well controlled with nitroglycerin comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of intermittent erectile dysfunction. He tells the physician that he no longer feels like a real man and is too embarrassed to discuss the situation with his wife. He underwent successful coronary artery bypass grafting 5 years ago. Medications include one aspirin each morning. He asks the physician for a prescription for sildenafil. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: A. "Episodic impotence is normal for a man your age."

options.label: B
options.html: B. "It is better if you try a testosterone patch first."

options.label: C
options.html: C. "Sildenafil is expensive, and your insurance is unlikely to cover the cost."

options.label: D
options.html: D. "Sildenafil may have harmful side effects for you."

options.label: E
options.html: E. "Your wife should be informed if you want to try sildenafil."

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Nitroglycerin and sildenafil should not be taken together, as this combination can cause potentially fatal hypotension. Thus, the most appropriate initial response by the physician is to advise the patient that sildenafil may have harmful effects for him.

Key Concept: When patients request a high-risk intervention, physicians should directly discuss the risks and consider withholding medications for which the risks outweigh the benefits.

Explanation: When obtaining informed consent from a patient, physicians should discuss four essential elements: the nature of the intervention, the risks, the benefits, and the alternatives. If the potential risks outweigh the potential benefits, the physician should consider withholding the intervention. As the combination of sildenafil and nitrates can cause potentially fatal hypotension, their use together is strictly contraindicated. The physician should explain this risk as a justification for withholding sildenafil.

Differential: Physicians should discuss alternative treatments if the requested treatment has the potential to cause harm. However, they should first explain why they cannot fulfill the patient’s original request.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: "Episodic impotence is normal for a man your age" is inappropriate. Though erectile dysfunction is somewhat common as patients age, it is treatable. Also, as the patient is requesting a specific treatment, the physician should address the patient’s request.

Choice B: "It is better if you try a testosterone patch first" is incorrect. The physician should discuss alternative treatments, but first they should address the patient’s request for sildenafil.

Choice C: "Sildenafil is expensive, and your insurance is unlikely to cover the cost" is inaccurate, as sildenafil is relatively inexpensive. Also, cost is not a strict contraindication. Though the costs of medications should be discussed, physicians should offer effective, low-risk treatments regardless of cost.

Choice E: "Your wife should be informed if you want to try sildenafil" is inappropriate. Patients are not required to inform anyone about the medications they are taking.

questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has had progressive fatigue and weakness over the past several months. Examination indicates both cardiac and skeletal muscle involvement. Microscopic examination of skeletal muscle tissue obtained on biopsy shows ragged red fibers. The most likely cause of his condition is a defect in which of the following organelles?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Educational Objective: Mitochondrial diseases may present with variable symptoms but often includes fatigue and primarily proximal muscle weakness. The most common abnormality identified on skeletal muscle tissue analysis in cases of mitochondrial myopathy is identification of ragged red fibers.

Evaluation: Musculoskeletal manifestations of mitochondrial myopathy include muscle pain, fatigue, exercise intolerance, and increased activities of creatine kinase, while potential neurologic symptoms may include ophthalmoplegia, seizures, myoclonus, and peripheral neuropathy. Cardiac manifestations include hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and heart failure.

Definition: Mitochondria are the cellular organelles that produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) via oxidative phosphorylation, a process that requires four enzyme complexes to produce a transmembrane potential that is ultimately used to produce ATP via ATP synthase. Mitochondrial DNA is separate from somatic nuclear DNA, and mutations in genes encoding any of these complexes can result in the failure of oxidative phosphorylation, which results in a subsequent failure to generate ATP, and consequential myopathy and neurologic symptoms. Mitochondrial diseases are strictly inherited through the mother, as sperm do not contain mitochondria to contribute to the fertilized embryo. Due to the failure of energy metabolism, the cells may compensate by producing additional mitochondria. On muscle biopsy, these mitochondrial aggregates, when visualized on the background of the myofibers, appear as ragged red fibers.

Prevention: There are no known ways to prevent mitochondrial disease. Mitochondrial disease is inherited from the mother.

Treatment: There is no proven way to effectively treat primary mitochondrial disorders.

Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with progressive fatigue and weakness with cardiac and skeletal muscle involvement. Examination of skeletal muscle tissue identified ragged red fibers which is the most common abnormality identified in cases of mitochondrial myopathy.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Choice A: Golgi complex is incorrect. Defects of the Golgi complex have been associated with conditions such as Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The mitochondria are more likely to have a defect in this case.

Choice B: Lysosome is incorrect. The lysosome has been identified to have defects in lysosomal storage diseases. These include conditions such as Krabbe disease, Tay-Sachs disease, and Fabry disease.

Choice D: Peroxisome is incorrect. Defects in peroxisome function may result in conditions such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, Zellweger syndrome, and infantile Refsum disease. A defect in the mitochondria is more likely in this case.

Choice E: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is incorrect. The endoplasmic reticulum has been identified to have a possible role in the development of many conditions such as multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, prion disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The findings in this patient make a defect in the mitochondria more likely.
